title: Loading & vessel departure
sceneDesc: A container ship arrives at the quay. A terminal truck brings the container under a giant quay crane, which lifts it on board. Lashers secure the stack and the ship sails.

narration.1: My ship {vessel} arrives at the quay. A terminal truck brings me under a giant [[quay-crane|quay crane]].
narration.2: {vessel} berths in its window; terminal tractors bring boxes from the yard in the crane sequence built from the stowage plan. [TO VERIFY:v61]
narration.3: Berth window and crane intensity are agreed between carrier and terminal; a late vessel compresses the window and can leave boxes behind ('cut and run'). [TO VERIFY:v61]

narration.1: Up I go! The crane lifts me high and places me exactly where the plan says.
narration.2: Loading: the crane driver places the box in its planned slot; the terminal tallies every move and updates the bay plan. [TO VERIFY:v62]
narration.3: Discrepancies (box loaded in wrong slot, overstow) are fixed or recorded; the final BAPLIE goes to the carrier and the next ports. [TO VERIFY:v61]

1.reefer: Workers fix me with steel bars and plug me into the ship's electricity, so I stay cold.
1.*: Workers secure me with steel bars and locks, so I don't move when the sea gets rough.

2.reefer: [[lashing|Lashing]] by terminal lashers; the reefer is plugged into a ship's socket and checked. [TO VERIFY:v57]
2.tank: Lashing, and DG stowage checked against the IMDG segregation and the DG manifest. [TO VERIFY:v59]
2.oog: Special lashing for OOG cargo, often on top of the stack or in dedicated slots. [TO VERIFY:v58]
2.*: [[lashing|Lashing]] with twistlocks, bars and turnbuckles by terminal lashers, per the ship's lashing plan. [TO VERIFY:v62]

narration.3: Lashing forces depend on stack weight distribution — another reason VGMs and correct stowage matter. Inadequate lashing is a known factor in container losses. [TO VERIFY:v77]

narration.1: The ship sails! Now that I'm on board, the carrier can issue the [[bl|Bill of Lading]] saying I'm 'shipped on board'.
narration.2: After loading, documentation issues the shipped-on-board B/L (or annotates a received B/L) and finalises the [[manifest]]. [TO VERIFY:v50]
narration.3: On-board date and vessel must be true: they're checked against L/C terms. Freight prepaid originals are often released only after payment. [TO VERIFY:v33] [TO VERIFY:v50]
The day after sailing, the shipper asks to correct the consignee's name, misspelled on the B/L. The three originals were already issued and couriered to the shipper's bank.

text.1: A quay crane can move a container every one to two minutes. [TO VERIFY:v62]
text.2: Each quay crane typically makes about 25–35 moves per hour; big ships work several cranes at once. [TO VERIFY:v62]

body.1: The giant crane that lifts containers between the quay and the ship.
body.2: Ship-to-shore (STS) cranes reach across 20+ container rows on the largest ships; productivity drives berth time and cost. [TO VERIFY:v62]

body.1: {vessel} — a container ship sailing from {pol} to {pod}.
body.2: Ship sizes depend on the lane: ultra-large ships on Asia–North Europe, smaller ones on lanes with shallower ports or canals. [TO VERIFY:v11] [TO VERIFY:v64]

body.1: Steel bars and locks keep stacked containers in place during the voyage.
body.2: Twistlocks between tiers, lashing bars and turnbuckles; responsibility for lashing lies with the ship/terminal, but cargo inside the box is the shipper's (SLAC). [TO VERIFY:v62]
body.3: Losses at sea are rare relative to volumes but occur in heavy weather, often with misdeclared weights or lashing failures. [TO VERIFY:v77]

body.1: On board, I'm plugged into the ship's electricity.
body.2: Ships have a limited number of reefer plugs — one reason reefer bookings need approval. Crew check reefers daily or monitor remotely. [TO VERIFY:v57]

body.1: Now that I'm loaded, the carrier issues the Bill of Lading: proof that it received me on board, and — for a 'to order' B/L — the 'key' to collect me at destination.

rows.label: Consignee
rows.value: To order of Demo Trade Bank (fictional)

1.2: The on-board notation (date, vessel, port) makes it a 'shipped on board' B/L — what most L/Cs require. [TO VERIFY:v50]

2.2: A full set of originals; at destination, one original (endorsed if 'to order') is surrendered to obtain release, and the others become void. [TO VERIFY:v68]

3.2: Signed by or for the carrier (or the master/agent). Place and date of issue are checked by banks.

2.prompt: What makes this a 'shipped on board' B/L?

options.text: The on-board notation with the date and vessel

options.fb: Freight terms don't say whether the goods are on board.
The number of originals is unrelated.
That makes it negotiable, not 'on board'.

2.explain: A 'shipped on board' B/L (or a 'received' B/L annotated on board) proves loading on a named vessel at a date — key for letters of credit. [TO VERIFY:v50]

3.prompt: The L/C requires shipment no later than Day 6. The on-board date is {etd}. What now?

options.text: The documents are discrepant: the shipper must seek an L/C amendment or the buyer's waiver — the B/L date stays true
Re-date the B/L to Day 6 as a courtesy
Issue a second B/L dated Day 6
options.fb: Two B/Ls for one shipment is fraud too.
Banks check dates strictly under UCP 600.

3.explain: UCP 600 banks examine dates strictly; the commercial fix is an L/C amendment or waiver, never a false B/L. [TO VERIFY:v50]

documents: **Shipped-on-board B/L** — or received B/L annotated on board. [TO VERIFY:v50]
**Final bay plan (BAPLIE)** and load report. [TO VERIFY:v61]
**Manifest** — cargo list for customs at the next ports.
costs: **Ocean freight** — prepaid now, or collect at destination ({freightTerms}).
risks: **Cut and run** — a late vessel sails without some boxes.
**B/L errors** after issuance → recall originals, amendment fee, L/C problems.
**Lashing failure** in heavy weather → cargo loss. [TO VERIFY:v77]
**Antedated B/L** → fraud exposure, loss of carrier defences.
jobs: **Vessel operations** — berth windows, port calls, ETA updates.
**Finance / credit control** — prepaid freight before release of originals. [TO VERIFY:v33]

incoNote.C: Under C-rules the risk passes here, on board — but the seller keeps paying costs to destination.

1: A quay crane loads me onto the ship following the plan.
Lashing keeps the stacks in place during the voyage.
Once I'm on board, the carrier issues the Bill of Lading.
2: Only boxes on the load list are loaded, in the planned crane sequence.
Lashing and stowage are the ship's job; cargo securing inside the box is the shipper's.
The shipped-on-board B/L proves loading on a named vessel and date.
3: B/L dates and vessels must be true — L/C problems are solved commercially, never by antedating.
Amending an issued negotiable B/L requires the full set of originals back.
Under FOB/CFR/CIF, risk passes on board here.

1.prompt: I'm on board and the ship has sailed. What happens next?

hint.yes: My first ship is a small one — I'll change ship on the way.
hint.*: There's a whole ocean between me and {pod}.

text.yes: I sail to the hub in {hub}, change ship, then cross to {pod}.

confirm.yes: Exactly. A feeder takes me to {hub}, where I'm transshipped onto a big mainline ship to {pod}.
confirm.*: Exactly. The voyage takes {transit}; the carrier tracks the ship and updates the arrival date.

options.text: I'm delivered to the customer the next day.
options.why: The ship has an ocean to cross first.
options.realLife: Even the fastest services take weeks between continents.
options.whenRight: Short-sea or domestic services can take a day or two — not this route.

options.text: I'm unloaded at the next port and checked by customs there.
options.why: Ships call at several ports, but I stay on board until my port of discharge (unless transshipped).
options.realLife: Boxes not due at a port stay on board; unloading the wrong box costs a lot.
options.whenRight: Only for boxes destined for that port.

2.prompt: {vessel} has sailed with the box on board; B/L issued. What happens next?

text.yes: Feeder voyage to {hub}, discharge and transshipment onto the mainline vessel, then the long-haul leg to {pod}.
text.*: Ocean voyage to {pod} ({transit}); the carrier monitors the voyage and sends the arrival notice before arrival.

confirm.yes: Correct. At the hub the box is discharged, stacked and reloaded onto {vessel}; missed connections are the main risk. [TO VERIFY:v73]
confirm.*: Correct. Transit depends on routing (Suez, Cape, Panama) and port rotation. [TO VERIFY:v10] [TO VERIFY:v63]

options.text: The consignee lodges the import declaration on board.
options.why: Import declarations are lodged with destination customs, typically when the goods arrive or shortly before.
options.realLife: Early lodging is possible in some regimes, but nothing is done 'on board'.
options.whenRight: Pre-arrival lodging exists in some regimes. [TO VERIFY:v67]

options.text: The original B/L is surrendered to the carrier at departure.
options.why: Originals go to the shipper (and banks) and are surrendered at destination to get release.
options.realLife: Surrendering at origin = express (telex) release, a deliberate choice.
options.whenRight: When the shipper chooses express release, originals are surrendered at origin.

options.text: The ENS is filed now that the vessel has sailed.
options.why: For deep-sea containers, the ENS is due before loading at origin.
options.realLife: Filing after loading would already have triggered problems. [TO VERIFY:v23]
options.whenRight: Other transport modes have different deadlines.

3.prompt: Case: the consignee's name is misspelled on an issued B/L; the 3/3 originals are already at the bank. What is the correct procedure?

options.text: Retrieve the full set of 3/3 originals, cancel them and reissue a corrected set (amendment fee); update the manifest and advance filings.
options.confirm: Right. A negotiable B/L can only be amended against surrender of the full set, otherwise two valid documents would circulate. Manifest/ICS2 data must be corrected too. [TO VERIFY:v12] [TO VERIFY:v68]

options.text: Issue a corrected B/L now; the old one will be ignored.
options.why: Two valid negotiable sets would circulate.
options.realLife: Risk of double claims and misdelivery.
options.whenRight: Never while the original set is outstanding.

options.text: Correct only the manifest; leave the B/L as it is.
options.why: B/L and manifest must match, and the bank will see the error.
options.realLife: Release problems at destination and L/C discrepancies.
options.whenRight: Only for data that isn't on the B/L.

options.text: Send the bank a letter saying the name is wrong.
options.why: A letter doesn't change a document of title.
options.realLife: The bank will still treat the B/L as presented.
options.whenRight: Never as a substitute for reissuing.
